new_statements.quote: [p.19] El acento de la palabra en inga es muy regular; en general, recae en la penúltima sílaba de cada palabra. Hay dos clases de excepciones: en primer lugar, al agregar ciertos sufijos a una palabra, el acento queda en la misma sílaba donde recaería, si no se hubiera agregado este sufijo (véanse los apéndices a las lecciones 1, 2, 3 y 4); en segundo lugar, el acento cae en la última sílaba de ciertas formas del verbo (por ejemplo, la tercera persona singular del presente habitual, y el imperativo singular). [p.36] Tal como los sufijos -ca/c y -pas, al agregar los sufijos -chu, -mi a una palabra, siempre que no sea un verbo, el acento no cae en la penúltima sílaba, sino que queda donde caería, si no hubiera estos sufijos: TANda 'pan', TANdami, TANdachu. No se aplica esta regla a los verbos: ruRA 'hace', ruRA(N)mi, ruRANchu.
new_statements.translation: [p.19] Word stress in Inga is very regular; in general it falls on the penultimate syllable of each word. There are two classes of exceptions: first, when certain suffixes are added to a word, the stress stays on the syllable where it would fall if the suffix had not been added (see the appendices to lessons 1, 2, 3 and 4); second, the stress falls on the last syllable of certain verb forms (for example, the third person singular of the habitual present, and the singular imperative). [p.36] Just like the suffixes -ca/c and -pas, when -chu, -mi are added to a word that is not a verb, the stress does not fall on the penultimate syllable but stays where it would fall without these suffixes: TANda 'bread', TANdami, TANdachu. This rule does not apply to verbs: ruRA 'does', ruRA(N)mi, ruRANchu.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Default penultimate stress. Two grammatically defined exception classes: (a) the enclitic suffixes -ca/-c, -pas, -chu, -mi, -si, -ta are invisible to stress on non-verbs (stress stays where it fell on the host, giving surface antepenult forms such as ímatac, huásipas, maymándata, cahuáspapas); on verbs the same suffixes count and stress moves to the new penult (ruRA > ruRA(N)mi, ruRANchu; saMUcu > samuCUNsi); (b) certain verb forms carry final stress (3sg habitual present, singular imperative): rurá, randí, pusá, atún, huañuchí, purinacú, chasquiy, micuy. Exercise 10 (pp.19-20) gives three word lists labelled penultimate, final and pre-penultimate stress. The orthography marks stress with a tilde by Spanish rules. No syllable-weight criterion is stated.
new_statements.exceptions: (1) Clitic suffixes -ca/-c, -pas (p.26), -chu, -mi (p.36), -ta (PDF 47-48), -si (p.67) do not shift stress on non-verbs; on verbs they do. (2) Final stress in 3sg habitual present and singular imperative (p.19). (3) p.136 note: in the compound tense with the modal suffix before the infinitive (Cáyachu cutimúngapa cangui?) 'el acento cae en la pre-penúltima sílaba'. (4) Dialect notes: Santiago speakers drop the clitic vowel (Tándam ca, Tándach ca) and the authors say this vowel loss 'probablemente tiene algo que ver con la posición del acento, ya que cae en la antepenúltima sílaba de la palabra' (p.36); the emphatic -sic/-mic forms are Santiago only (p.67).
new_statements.identity_note: All three works describe Highland Inga of the Sibundoy Valley (Putumayo), distinguishing the Santiago and San Andrés dialects (1978 title: 'Valle de Sibundoy, Intendencia del Putumayo'; 1981 marks forms 'Sant' vs 'S.A.'). The 1981 grammar notes Santiago-only clitic vowel loss (Tándam ca) and -sic/-mic emphatics, and San Andrés-only -pas > -s and y > h after i; the accent rule itself is stated for the language as a whole. None covers the Jungle Inga (inj) variety.

new_statements.translation: [p.3] Word stress in Inga generally falls on the penultimate syllable. To make reading easier we use the acute accent according to the rules of Spanish. [p.13] Notes: *When certain endings are added (e.g. -cuna, plural of the 3rd person), an n appears. Otherwise the stress falls on the last syllable.

new_statements.translation: [p.2] Word stress in Inga is very regular; as a general rule it falls on the penultimate syllable of each word. To make reading easier the stress is generally marked following the same rules as in Spanish (that is, for the so-called 'regular' stress: the stress will be on the penultimate syllable when the word ends in a vowel, n or s; it will be on the last syllable when the word ends in some consonant other than n and s, in which case it is not marked. All 'irregular' occurrences are marked). [...] PUANgui. aLLIsia. cayaCAma. PUANguichi. [p.7] -ca, -ta never affect the stressed syllable of the words they attach to. -mi, on the other hand, affects the stressed syllable only if the word it attaches to is a verb: NUca MAYma huaSIma but: ricUni / NUcaca MAYmata huaSImami ricuNImi.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Penultimate stress as the general rule; the clitics -ca and -ta never shift the host's stress, -mi shifts it only on verbs. A later lesson (scanned only) notes that the 3sg subject is marked by stress on the last syllable of the root. The scanned text of p.7 also says '-ca es un sufijo que indica acento secundario en las palabras a las cuales está adherido' (not re-verified on the page image).
new_statements.secondary_stress: -ca is described (p.7, scanned text) as a suffix that 'indica acento secundario' on the word it attaches to.
new_statements.exceptions: Clitics -ca, -ta (and -chu, -si, -char) do not affect the host's stress; -mi affects stress on verbs only. 3sg forms take stress on the last root syllable (catuni / catungui / catí paradigm, the scanned text). 'Algunos instructores del dialecto 2 omiten el -pa, de suerte que el acento recae sobre -nga' (the scanned text).

audit.recode_to: weight (quantity-sensitive, right edge: final if the word-final syllable is closed by a sonorant /m n r y/, else penultimate; antepenult when certain suffixes/enclitics are word-final (níspaka, ímata; -ka/-ta/-mi on substantives outside the domain); 3sg -n ~ accented final vowel; a very small set of lexical exceptions (mánčay, arí); optional alternating secondary counting leftward from the primary). Deciding source should become Levinsohn 1979:82-83 (= Levinsohn 1976 phonology chapter), strength of the evidence page-image, with Levinsohn 1974:2,7 retained as supporting. what counts as heavy stays sonorant-closed CVC; 'heavy' field should quote 'C 300 = /m, n, r, y/' instead of 'no weight criterion is stated'. The StressTyp2 'contra' note softens: StressTyp2's U/P with sonorant-coda heavy reproduces Levinsohn's own statement; the residual disagreements in E/V's tally are the clitic and 3sg cases Levinsohn himself lists as grammatical conditioning, plus Maffla's Santiago-dialect glide-final forms.

audit.reasoning: (1) The deciding quotation is verbatim on the page image we hold of Levinsohn 1974 p.2 and the p.7 clitic passage is in the held scanned; quote check passes. (2) But the classification 'weight-hedged' exists only because the 1974 pedagogical grammar states no weight criterion and the reader could not reach Levinsohn 1976; the weight rule was attributed to Hayes 1995/StressTyp2 as 'carried'. The primary describer's phonology (Levinsohn 1979 'Fonología del inga', SFIC IV:65-85, the Spanish version of the 1976 Mouton phonology chapter) has been sitting in since 2026-09-13 and states the criterion outright on p.82: final accent when the last syllable ends in /m n r y/, antepenult with certain word-final suffixes, otherwise penult; phonemic but grammatically predictable; few lexical exceptions; optional alternating secondary. sources.quote: 'El acento primario ... cae en la penúltima, antepenúltima o última sílaba. Es fonémico, pero gramaticalmente predecible. Cuando la última sílaba de una palabra gramatical termina en (C 300), el acento cae sobre la última sílaba. (C 300 = /m, n, r, y/.) /yawár/ 'sangre', /mančáy/ 'temer'. Un número muy reducido de palabras no siguen esta regla: /mánčay/ 'temor', /arí/ 'sí'. ... [3sg] /-n/ ~ /-´Ø/: /kawarín/ ~ [kawarí] 'apareció'. ... Cuando ciertos sufijos ocurren en posición final de palabra ... el acento cae sobre la antepenúltima sílaba: /níspaka/, /ímata/. En los demás casos el acento cae
